> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

`contracts/receipt-anchor/src/fuzz_test.rs` contains one test. The refund vault's has
two. Issues #16 and #29 asked for fuzz testing of `RefundVault` edge cases and TTL
extension boundaries respectively, and what landed is a thin sample of the state space.

The contracts have genuinely interesting state machines that reward property testing
over example testing:

- **`ReceiptAnchor` pruning** maintains a `PrunedUpTo` cursor and the README promises
  the deleted range *"always stays a contiguous prefix — a batch is never removed from
  the middle while older ones remain readable."* That is a property, stated in prose,
  enforced by example tests. It should be a fuzz invariant.
- **`RefundVault` float accounting** must satisfy `float == deposits - refunds -
  withdrawals` after any sequence of operations.
- **Merkle verification** must reject every proof that is not the correct one, which is
  a universally-quantified claim that example tests can only sample.

## What to build

**Property-based tests with generated operation sequences.** State the invariant, then
generate randomised sequences and assert it holds after each step.

**Invariants to pin, at minimum:**

| Contract | Invariant |
|---|---|
| `ReceiptAnchor` | pruned batches always form a contiguous prefix; `PrunedUpTo` is monotonic |
| `ReceiptAnchor` | `get_batch_count` equals the number of `anchor_batch` calls, regardless of pruning |
| `ReceiptAnchor` | `verify_receipt` returns true **only** for leaves actually in the tree — generate wrong leaves, wrong proofs, truncated proofs, proofs from a different batch, and proofs with swapped sibling order (which the sorted-pair convention should make irrelevant — assert that) |
| `RefundVault` | float never negative; float equals deposits minus refunds minus withdrawals |
| `RefundVault` | a `payment_ref` is refundable at most once under any interleaving |
| `RefundVault` | operations while paused never mutate state |
| Both | TTL extension never shortens a TTL; extension on a missing record always errors |

**Seed corpus.** When a fuzz run finds a failure, add the failing input as a permanent
example test. A property test that finds a bug once and forgets it has done half its
job.

Note the constraint: these run inside the Soroban test environment, so the practical
approach is generated operation sequences driven by a seeded PRNG rather than a
coverage-guided fuzzer. Document the approach and its limits.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every invariant in the table is a property test over generated sequences
- [ ] Sequence length and iteration count are tunable, with CI running a bounded budget
      and a longer profile available locally
- [ ] Any failure found is added as a permanent regression test
- [ ] The Merkle rejection property covers wrong leaf, wrong proof, wrong length, wrong
      batch, and sibling-order permutation
- [ ] The approach and its limits are documented in the test module header
title: test: expand fuzz coverage beyond the current three cases

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

`RefundVault` deals in `i128` amounts with `AmountExceedsMax` and `InvalidAmount`
errors and a `RefundMax` storage key. Stellar assets carry **7 decimals**, so a "5 USDC"
refund is `50_000_000`. Every amount crossing the boundary between a merchant-facing
system and this contract goes through that conversion, and decimal handling is
consistently the most common integration bug in payment systems.

What is not currently pinned anywhere:

- what `RefundMax` is denominated in, and how it relates to 7-decimal units
- the behaviour at the arithmetic boundaries — `i128` overflow in the float accounting,
  a refund of exactly the remaining float, a refund of 1 stroop, a refund of 0
- whether `overflow-checks = true` in the release profile actually protects the paths
  that matter (it is set in `Cargo.toml`, which is good — but a test should prove the
  path panics rather than wraps)

The two fuzz tests currently in the repo (`fuzz_test.rs` in each contract) are a start
but do not cover the decimal semantics.

## What to build

**Boundary tests on `RefundVault`:**

- refund of exactly the available float succeeds; float + 1 fails with
  `InsufficientFloat`
- refund of `0` and of a negative amount fail with `InvalidAmount`
- refund of `1` (one stroop) succeeds and accounts correctly
- `RefundMax` at the boundary: exactly max succeeds, max + 1 fails with
  `AmountExceedsMax`
- deposits summing near `i128::MAX` panic on overflow rather than wrapping — assert the
  panic, do not assume the profile setting covers it
- a sequence of many small refunds sums exactly, with no accumulated drift

**Documentation:**

- state in the README that all amounts are in the token's smallest unit (stroops for
  7-decimal assets), with a worked USDC example — `5 USDC → 50_000_000`
- state what `RefundMax` and `refund_window_ledgers` are denominated in; ledgers are not
  seconds and `17280` in `deployments/testnet.env` deserves its arithmetic shown
  (~5s/ledger → ~24 hours)

**Extend the fuzz tests** to generate amounts across the full `i128` range, including
values near the bounds, and assert the invariant that vault float never goes negative
and never exceeds total deposits minus total refunds and withdrawals.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every boundary case above is a named test
- [ ] Overflow behaviour is asserted, not assumed from the profile setting
- [ ] The float accounting invariant is fuzz-checked
- [ ] README documents amount units with a worked USDC example
- [ ] `refund_window_ledgers` documented in ledgers with the time conversion shown
title: test: pin 7-decimal amount handling and the `i128` bounds on vault arithmetic

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

Neither contract carries build metadata. Given a contract id on testnet — the two in
`DEPLOYMENTS.md` — there is no on-chain way to answer "which commit of this repo is
that?". Reconciling a deployed contract with its source is currently a matter of trust
plus a wasm hash comparison someone has to do by hand.

There is also no versioning policy. `Cargo.toml` at the workspace root declares no
version for the contracts, there are no git tags, and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` records contract
ids without recording what was deployed.

## What to do

**1. `contractmeta!` in both contracts** with at minimum:

```rust
contractmeta!(key = "name", val = "ReceiptAnchor");
contractmeta!(key = "version", val = env!("CARGO_PKG_VERSION"));
contractmeta!(key = "repo", val = "https://github.com/accensa/accensa-contracts");
contractmeta!(key = "commit", val = env!("GIT_SHA"));
```

The commit SHA needs a `build.rs` to supply it; keep that build script minimal and make
it degrade gracefully outside a git checkout (a source tarball build must not fail).

**2. Versions in `Cargo.toml`** for both contract crates, starting from the current
state. Decide semver semantics for a contract and write them down — what counts as a
breaking change when the interface is a set of exported functions and event schemas?
(Event topics are part of that surface; see #51.)

**3. Record deployments properly.** `deployments/testnet.env` currently holds contract
ids and no provenance. Add the version, commit SHA and wasm hash of what was deployed,
and make `deploy.sh` write them automatically so it cannot be forgotten.

**4. A `docs/RELEASING.md`**: how a version is cut, tagged, built reproducibly, and
recorded in `DEPLOYMENTS.md`.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Both contracts embed name, version, repo and commit metadata
- [ ] `build.rs` supplies the SHA and degrades gracefully without git
- [ ] Contract crates carry versions; semver semantics documented
- [ ] `deploy.sh` records version, commit and wasm hash into the deployment env file
- [ ] `docs/RELEASING.md` exists
- [ ] The currently-deployed testnet contracts are reconciled to a commit, and that is
      recorded in `DEPLOYMENTS.md`
title: chore: add `contractmeta!` version metadata and a release/versioning policy

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

`contracts/receipt-anchor/src/vectors.rs` is shared between this Rust contract and the
TypeScript SDK in `accensa/accensa-app`, so `verifyReceipt` is proven to agree across
two independent implementations. This is the strongest single artifact this repo owns —
cross-implementation conformance demonstrated rather than asserted, against a grading
criterion whose stated failure mode is *drift, not inability*.

And it is enforced by **nothing automated across the two repos**. There is a Rust-side
test (`test_shared_vectors_match_typescript_sdk`) that checks the Rust implementation
against the vectors. There is no mechanism that fails when:

- someone edits `vectors.rs` here and the SDK is never updated
- someone changes the SDK's hashing and this repo never learns
- the two copies of the vector file silently diverge

The proof-of-parity is only as good as the process keeping the two in sync, and right
now that process is "remember to".

## What to build

**1. A single source of truth for the vectors.** Decide and document which repo owns
`vectors.rs` and how the other consumes it. Options, in rough order of preference:

- publish the vectors as a versioned data file (JSON) that both repos import, with a
  content hash committed on each side
- keep the Rust file authoritative and generate the TypeScript fixture from it in CI

Whichever is chosen, **a divergence must fail a build**, not produce a warning.

**2. A cross-repo CI check.** A job here that fetches the SDK's vector fixture (pinned
by ref) and fails if the content hash differs from ours. A matching job in
`accensa-app` doing the reverse. A repository-dispatch or scheduled run is acceptable;
silence is not.

**3. Extend the vectors.** The convention is sorted-pair SHA-256, so proofs carry no
position flags. The edge cases that break naive implementations should all be in the
set: single-leaf trees, two-leaf, odd leaf counts requiring promotion, duplicate leaves,
the sorted-pair tie case where both siblings hash identically, and a proof of the wrong
length. Each of these is a real way the two implementations can disagree.

**4. Document it** in `docs/ADR-001-merkle-structure.md` or a new
`docs/CONFORMANCE.md`: the parity mechanism, what it guarantees, and what it does not.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A single authoritative vector source, with the ownership decision documented
- [ ] A CI job fails when the two repos' vectors diverge
- [ ] The corresponding job exists in `accensa-app` (link the PR)
- [ ] Vector set extended to cover single/two/odd/duplicate-leaf and tie cases
- [ ] Parity mechanism documented, including its limits
title: ci: enforce Rust/TypeScript vector parity for `verify_receipt` on every push

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

CI runs fmt, clippy, test and `cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release`. Nothing
checks what the build *costs*. Soroban enforces hard per-transaction limits on CPU
instructions, memory, ledger reads and writes, and a contract that grows past them
fails at invocation time — on-chain, in front of a user, not in CI.

This repo has a concrete exposure: `anchor_batch` accepts up to
`MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 1000`, and `prune_batches` walks forward deleting records. Both scale
with input. Issue #20 benchmarked large batch anchors once; nothing prevents a
regression tomorrow.

**We have the tooling for this and it is our own.** `Tollcraft/soroban-cost-linter`
(Apache-2.0) and `Tollcraft/soroban-budget-assert` are exactly resource-limit and
budget-measurement tooling for Soroban. Using our own tools on our own contracts is
both the right technical answer and a demonstration that they work.

## What to build

**A `budget` CI job** that fails the build on regression:

1. **Wasm size ceiling** per contract, with the current size committed as the baseline
   and a stated tolerance. Wasm size drives deployment cost and is the easiest signal
   to track.
2. **Budget assertions** via `soroban-budget-assert` on the operations that scale:
   - `anchor_batch` at `count = 1`, at a midpoint, and at `MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 1000`
   - `verify_receipt` across proof depths (a 1000-leaf tree means a 10-element proof)
   - `prune_batches` over a large deletable range
   - `refund` and `deposit` on `RefundVault`
   Each with a committed budget baseline and a failure threshold.
3. **`soroban-cost-linter`** over both contracts, with findings surfaced in the job
   output.
4. **Published numbers.** Write the measured budgets into `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` — CPU
   instructions, memory, reads, writes per function, with the headroom against the
   network limit stated as a percentage. Headroom is the number that tells a reader
   whether `MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 1000` is a safe constant or a lucky one.

**Baselines must be committed and updated deliberately.** A budget check whose baseline
is regenerated automatically on every run checks nothing.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] A `budget` job in `.github/workflows/ci.yml` fails on wasm-size or budget
      regression beyond a stated threshold
- [ ] Both Tollcraft tools are integrated, with their versions pinned
- [ ] Baselines committed to the repo and updated only by an explicit change
- [ ] `docs/BENCHMARKS.md` publishes per-function CPU, memory, read and write costs
      with headroom against network limits
- [ ] The `MAX_BATCH_SIZE = 1000` constant is justified by a measured number rather
      than by assertion — and adjusted if the measurement says it should be
- [ ] README links to the benchmarks
title: ci: enforce wasm size and resource-budget limits with the Tollcraft Soroban tooling

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

The events emitted by these contracts are a **public interface**. `README.md` documents
them as such, and states that the `AnchorEvent` and `RefundEvent` data maps mirror
`BatchRecord` and `RefundRecord` "so an indexer decodes it with the same shape
`get_batch` returns".

Nothing enforces that. There is a `test_events_emitted` and a
`test_anchor_and_prune_events_emitted`, but no test that pins the exact topic strings
and field names against a stated expectation. A field rename, a topic change, or a
divergence between the event data map and the record struct all compile cleanly, pass
the existing tests, and break every downstream indexer silently.

Silent indexer breakage is not hypothetical for this project — a previous indexer
outage ran for a week before anyone noticed, costing 207 permanently lost ledgers. The
cheapest defence is a test that fails the moment the wire shape changes.

## What to build

**Golden event tests.** For every event — `AnchorEvent`, `PruneEvent`, `DepositEvent`,
`RefundEvent`, `WithdrawEvent`:

- assert the exact topic tuple, with the topic strings written as literals in the test
  so a rename produces a diff a reviewer must consciously approve
- assert every data field name and type
- assert the data map is structurally identical to the record returned by the
  corresponding getter (`AnchorEvent` vs `get_batch`, `RefundEvent` vs `get_refund`),
  since the README promises exactly this

**An event reference document** — `docs/EVENTS.md` — generated or hand-written, giving
for each event the topics, the data schema, when it fires, and what an indexer should
do with it. The README tables then link here rather than duplicating.

**A stability policy.** State it plainly: event topics and field names are a public
interface; changing one is a breaking change requiring a major version and an
announcement. Then say what an indexer author should do about it — subscribe by topic,
tolerate unknown fields, and so on.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] Every event has a test asserting its exact topics and data field names
- [ ] Event data maps are asserted structurally equal to the corresponding getter
      returns
- [ ] `docs/EVENTS.md` documents all five events with firing conditions
- [ ] A stability policy is written down and referenced from `CONTRIBUTING.md`
- [ ] The tests fail if a topic string or field name is changed — demonstrate this
      during development

## Related

Depends on the topic-name question being settled by #50; do that one
first or resolve the discrepancy here.
title: test: pin event topics and data shapes as an indexer-facing contract

body:
> **Repo context.** `accensa-contracts` holds the on-chain half of Accensa: `ReceiptAnchor`
> (Merkle batch anchoring so an agent can verify it was charged correctly without trusting
> the seller's API) and `RefundVault` (policy-bounded refunds without the merchant becoming
> a custodian). Both are deployed on testnet and covered by 48 unit tests. `soroban-sdk`
> 27.0.4, MIT. See `README.md`, `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md` and `DEPLOYMENTS.md` before
> starting.

## Problem

The entire contents of `docs/storage-audit.md`:

```
# Storage Audit Conclusion\nAfter auditing the storage calls, it is determined that all state stored as `Persistent` is necessary and cannot be reconstructed. `BatchRecord` and `RefundRecord` serve as audit trails and must remain persistent. Instance storage like `DataKey::Admin`, `BatchCount`, `PrunedUpTo`, and the pause flag also belong there. No state can be moved to `Temporary`.
```

The `\n` sequences are **literal backslash-n characters**, not newlines — the file was
written by a tool that escaped them and it renders on GitHub as one unbroken line. It is
also a conclusion with no audit behind it: it states that every persistent entry is
necessary without showing the enumeration that would justify the claim.

This matters more than a typical formatting nit. Storage class selection drives rent
and archival, which is one of the genuine strengths this repo is cited for. A one-line
file asserting a conclusion is the weakest possible form of that evidence.

## What to write

Rewrite it as a real audit that a reader can check:

1. **An enumeration of every storage entry** in both contracts — key, storage class
   (Instance / Persistent / Temporary), what it holds, and its size characteristics.
   Read `contracts/receipt-anchor/src/lib.rs` and `contracts/refund-vault/src/lib.rs`
   for the `DataKey` variants; `RefundVault` alone has nine.
2. **Per entry, the justification** for its class. The question to answer for each is
   the one the current text answers only in aggregate: can this be reconstructed from
   events or chain history if it is lost? If yes, it should probably not be persistent.
3. **TTL strategy per entry.** `TTL_EXTEND` is 518,400 ledgers (~30 days) with a
   `TTL_THRESHOLD` of 100. State why per entry, not once globally.
4. **Rent cost implications** — what a merchant pays to keep N batches and M refund
   records alive, and how `prune_batches` changes that. Link to
   `docs/MAINNET_DEPLOYMENT.md`, which has fee/rent analysis.
5. **Archival and restore.** What actually happens when an entry is archived and how it
   is restored; the README's Storage Archival section covers the user-facing part and
   this should carry the mechanism.

## Acceptance criteria

- [ ] The file renders as proper markdown with real newlines
- [ ] Every `DataKey` variant in both contracts appears in the enumeration
- [ ] Each entry has a stated storage class, justification and TTL rationale
- [ ] Rent implications are quantified, not asserted
- [ ] The existing conclusion is either supported by the enumeration or revised
- [ ] Linked from `README.md` and `docs/SECURITY_MODEL.md`

## Good first issue

No contract changes — this is reading two `lib.rs` files carefully and writing down
what you find. It is one of the better ways to learn the codebase.
title: docs: `docs/storage-audit.md` is a single line of escaped text, not a document
